title: Ezra 8:1–14
context: Ezra lists the heads of fathers’ households who went up with him from Babylon. The list begins with two priestly lines and a descendant of David (8:2) and continues with twelve further entries, most naming a lay family, a leader, and the number of males with him (8:3–14). Most of the lay family names (such as Parosh, Pahathmoab, Elam, Adin, Bebai, Azgad, Adonikam, and Bigvai) also appear in the list of the first returnees in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, which suggests that further members of families already represented in Judah now joined them; the numbers in Ezra 8 are much smaller and describe a different group. In 8:5 and 8:10 the usual pattern of family name and leader is less clear in this text, and this page does not reconstruct it. Both traditions read the list as shared ground: God remembers by name those who answered the call to return and serve.

verses.text: Now these are the heads of their fathers’ households, and this is the genealogy of those who went up with me from Babylon, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king:
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra introduces the heads of fathers’ households who went up with him in the reign of Artaxerxes. Arminian readers note that the list honors those who chose to make the journey. Each family made a real decision to leave Babylon and join the work in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list as a record of those God gathered to return. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing a roll of willing participants, and both affirm that God remembers by name those who serve his purposes.

verses.text: Of the sons of Phinehas, Gershom. Of the sons of Ithamar, Daniel. Of the sons of David, Hattush.
verses.arminianNotes: Gershom of Phinehas, Daniel of Ithamar, and Hattush of David head the list. Arminian readers note that priests and a royal descendant join the return. A Hattush appears among David’s descendants in 1 Chronicles 3:22, though the text does not say whether he is the same man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the presence of priestly and Davidic families and see God keeping David’s line among his people after exile. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the restored community’s continuity with its priesthood and royal house, holding the identification of Hattush loosely.

verses.text: Of the sons of Shecaniah, of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah; and with him were listed by genealogy of the males one hundred fifty.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah goes up with 150 males. Arminian readers note that Parosh was also among the families of the first return (2:3). Relatives of earlier returnees now choose to join them, strengthening the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see continuity between the first return and Ezra’s company. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of a careful list that ties families together across generations, and neither builds a doctrinal point on the number.

verses.text: Of the sons of Pahathmoab, Eliehoenai the son of Zerahiah; and with him two hundred males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of Pahathmoab, Eliehoenai son of Zerahiah goes with 200 males. Arminian readers note that Pahathmoab was a large family in the first return (2:6). Another group from the same family now makes the journey, adding to its presence in Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the continuity with Ezra 2 and see God gathering more of his people over time. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the roll of returnees and see in it the gradual restoration of the community.

verses.text: Of the sons of Shecaniah, the son of Jahaziel; and with him three hundred males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Shecaniah, the son of Jahaziel goes with 300 males. Arminian readers note that the pattern of the list is less clear here, since the leader’s own name is not given in this text. They do not try to reconstruct it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise accept the verse as it stands and do not speculate beyond it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the list of those who went up, and both affirm the value of the record even where its details are not fully clear.

verses.text: Of the sons of Adin, Ebed the son of Jonathan; and with him fifty males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Adin, Ebed son of Jonathan goes with 50 males. Arminian readers note that Adin also appears in the first return (2:15). The smaller number shows that even modest groups were counted and honored in the record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the link with Ezra 2 and the care taken to record every group. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of a faithful roll and affirm that no contribution to God’s work is too small to be remembered.

verses.text: Of the sons of Elam, Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah; and with him seventy males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Elam, Jeshaiah son of Athaliah goes with 70 males. Arminian readers note the continuity with Elam in the first return (2:7). Athaliah here is a man’s name, not the queen of Judah, and the context makes that clear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the family connection with Ezra 2 and the common name. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the list of returnees, with no doctrinal question raised, and see in it the reunion of families in the land.

verses.text: Of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah the son of Michael; and with him eighty males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah son of Michael goes with 80 males. Arminian readers note that Shephatiah also appears in the first return (2:4). Another branch of the family now decides to join, which strengthens the community in Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God gathering further members of established families. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical record and affirm that the restoration unfolded in stages, with God bringing his people home over time.

verses.text: Of the sons of Joab, Obadiah the son of Jehiel; and with him two hundred eighteen males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Joab, Obadiah son of Jehiel goes with 218 males. Arminian readers note that Joab appears in Ezra 2:6 as part of the family of Pahathmoab. Here the descendants of Joab are listed as their own group, which the text does not explain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the connection with Ezra 2:6 and do not force a harmony. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the roll of returnees and accept that family groupings could be recorded differently in different lists.

verses.text: Of the sons of Shelomith, the son of Josiphiah; and with him one hundred sixty males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Shelomith, the son of Josiphiah goes with 160 males. Arminian readers note that, as in 8:5, the leader’s own name is not clearly given in this text. They read the verse as it stands and do not reconstruct the missing detail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise accept the verse without speculation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Ezra’s list, recognize that its pattern is less clear here, and affirm the value of the record of those who went up.

verses.text: Of the sons of Bebai, Zechariah the son of Bebai; and with him twenty-eight males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Bebai, Zechariah son of Bebai goes with 28 males. Arminian readers note that Bebai also appears in the first return (2:11). The family name repeated in the leader’s name shows how names were passed down in Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the continuity with Ezra 2 and the small size of the group. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical record and see in it a family keeping its identity across generations of exile and return.

verses.text: Of the sons of Azgad, Johanan the son of Hakkatan; and with him one hundred ten males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Azgad, Johanan son of Hakkatan goes with 110 males. Arminian readers note that Azgad was among the first returnees (2:12). Each family that joined Ezra represented a real decision to leave settled life in Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the continuity with the first return and God’s steady gathering of his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the roll of those who went up and affirm the faithfulness of families who answered the call.

verses.text: Of the sons of Adonikam, who were the last, their names are: Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah; and with them sixty males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Adonikam, “who were the last,” Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah go with 60 males. Arminian readers note that Adonikam appears in the first return (2:13). The phrase “who were the last” may mean the remaining members of the family, though the text does not explain it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the meaning of the phrase loosely and note the continuity with Ezra 2. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Ezra’s list and decline to build conclusions on an unclear expression.

verses.text: Of the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zabbud; and with them seventy males.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zabbud go with 70 males. Arminian readers note that Bigvai was also among the first returnees (2:14). The list closes with a family that, like most of the others, already had members in Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the continuity with Ezra 2 and see the list as a whole testifying to God’s gathering of his people in stages. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing verse as completing a roll of willing returnees whom God remembers by name.
